state.misconception_label: Thinks alternate angles are always equal

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are arguing about alternate angles. Tom says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate. Katie says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are equal. Who is correct? ![Shows two non parallel lines that are intersected by another line. Angles P and Q are both on the outside of the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.](). I got Only
Katie because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Actually, in this case, angles \( p \) and \( q \) are not necessarily equal. Alternate angles are not always equal; they are just congruent when the lines are parallel. Can you explain why angles \( p \) and \( q \) might not be equal in this scenario?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I see! So if the lines aren't parallel, then angles \( p \) and \( q \) can be different? But how do I know when the lines are parallel? Is there a way to tell just by looking at the angles?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Yes, that's correct! One way to tell if the lines are parallel is by looking at the angles. If the angles formed by the transversal are equal, then the lines are parallel. Remember, alternate angles are only equal when the lines they are on are parallel. Can you think of any other types of angles that might help us determine if the lines are parallel?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher directly addresses the misconception that alternate angles are always equal, but makes a problematic circular statement in Turn 3 (suggesting equal angles prove parallelism when that's what needs to be determined), and while the student shows some progress in understanding the role of parallel lines, the scaffolding could be more precise about the logical relationship between parallelism and angle equality.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher uses questioning and guided discovery rather than direct explanation with worked examples, which is inconsistent with the traditional strategy of explicitly explaining concepts and demonstrating solutions.
